keyVerseText: I will offer unto thee burnt sacrifices of fatlings, with the incense of rams; I will offer bullocks with goats. Selah. fatlings: Heb. marrow
rootMeaning: The root of מֵחַ (mêach) traces back to the Hebrew root מָחָה (mâchâh), which fundamentally means to stroke or rub, often with the implication of greasing or making fat. This etymology highlights a process of enriching or anointing, going beyond the simple English gloss of 'fatling' to suggest something that is carefully prepared or made rich, possibly by the application of oil or fat. Thus, the word carries connotations of abundance and choice quality, reflecting a state of being well-fattened or richly endowed.
usageInScripture: The word מֵחַ appears only twice in Scripture, consistently referring to 'fatlings' or 'fat ones.' It is used in the plural absolute form, emphasizing abundance or fullness, and is sometimes employed figuratively to denote richness or wealth. This consistency in translation as 'fatlings' or 'fat ones' underscores its association with sacrificial offerings and metaphorical richness, revealing a focus on something prized and valuable in both literal and figurative senses.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding מֵחַ as rooted in the notion of greasing or fatness enriches our grasp of biblical sacrifice and divine provision. Fatlings were considered the choicest offerings, symbolizing the best that one could present to God, which aligns with the biblical call to offer our best to Him. The figurative use of the term for 'rich men' points to the broader biblical theme of abundance entrusted by God. This word reminds believers of the richness of God’s grace and the call to live in a manner worthy of His generous provision, ultimately fulfilled in Christ who is the ultimate offering and richness to His people.
keyVerseReflection: In Psalms 66:15, the psalmist declares, 'I will offer unto thee burnt sacrifices of fatlings, with the incense of rams; I will offer bullocks with goats.' Here, מֵחַ as 'fatlings' emphasizes the offering of the choicest, richest sacrifices to God, symbolizing wholehearted devotion and thanksgiving. The term enriches the verse by highlighting the quality and value of what is given to God, reflecting a heart that desires to honor Him with the best, an attitude that foreshadows the perfect sacrifice of Christ.
